# 5.3 - Experiments {.unnumbered}

Does a new pill stop headaches? You could compare people who chose to take it with people who did not. But those two groups might be different in many ways: age, sleep, stress.

An {{< glink experiment >}} solves this. The researcher gives the treatment on purpose and compares groups that are alike.

:::{.objectives}
- [ ] I name the subjects, treatments, explanatory variable, and response variable in an experiment.
- [ ] I explain control groups, placebos, and blinding.
- [ ] I explain why random assignment matters.
- [ ] I describe a completely randomized design, a randomized block design, and a matched pairs design.
:::

### 5.3.1 - The Language of Experiments

| Word | In the headache experiment |
|---|---|
| Subjects (experimental units) | The 40 volunteers with headaches |
| {{< glink "explanatory variable" text="Explanatory variable" >}} | What we change: the type of pill |
| {{< glink treatment text="Treatments" >}} | The things we compare: new pill, placebo |
| {{< glink "response variable" text="Response variable" >}} | What we measure: headache relief |
| {{< glink "control group" text="Control group" >}} | The group that does not get the new treatment |
| {{< glink placebo text="Placebo" >}} | A fake treatment that looks real, like a sugar pill |
| {{< glink "double-blind" text="Double-blind" >}} | Neither the subjects nor the people measuring know who got which pill |

![](/images/Unit_5/5.3_design.svg){width="620px" fig-align="center"}

This is a {{< glink "completely randomized design" >}}. Chance alone decides which group each subject joins.

***

### 5.3.2 - Principles of a Good Experiment

:::{.remember title="Control, Random Assignment, Replication"}
- **Control:** Compare to a control group. Keep everything else the same for both groups.
- **Random assignment:** Use chance to put subjects into groups. Then the groups are about the same, except for the treatment.
- **{{< glink replication text="Replication" >}}:** Use many subjects. With more subjects, chance differences between the groups get smaller.
:::

:::{.think title="Why give the control group a placebo?"}
People often feel better just because they *think* they got medicine. This is the **placebo effect**. With a placebo, both groups think they are being treated. So any extra difference comes from the real pill.
:::

***

### 5.3.3 - Matched Pairs and Blocks

In a {{< glink "matched pairs" >}} design, each subject gets **both** treatments, in a random order. Or you pair up very similar subjects, like twins. Each twin gets a different treatment.

**Example:** Which running shoe is faster? Each runner runs once in each shoe. A coin flip decides which shoe goes first. Comparing each runner to themselves removes the differences between runners.

:::{.you-try title="Why flip a coin to decide which shoe goes first?"}
Runners might be tired on the second run, or warmed up. The coin keeps that from always helping the same shoe.
:::

In a {{< glink "randomized block design" >}}, first split the subjects into groups that are alike (**blocks**). Then randomly assign the treatments inside each block. Comparing inside each block keeps the differences between blocks out of the result.

**Example:** A gym tests two workout plans with 40 members. 16 members are beginners and 24 are experienced. Beginners usually get stronger faster.

- The blocks are the beginners and the experienced members.
- Inside each block, chance decides who gets each plan. 8 beginners and 12 experienced members get each plan.
- Compare the two plans inside each block.

![](/images/Unit_5/5.3_block_design.svg){width="620px" fig-align="center"}

:::{.you-try title="Why not just randomly assign all 40 members to the two plans?"}
Chance could put more beginners in one plan. That plan would look better because beginners get stronger faster, not because the plan is better. Blocks make sure each plan gets the same number of beginners.
:::

:::{.note title="Blocks and strata"}
A randomized block design works like a {{< glink "stratified sample" >}} (5.2). Both split people into groups that are alike. Then both use chance inside each group.

- **Stratified sample:** chance picks **who is in the sample**.
- **Randomized block design:** chance picks **which treatment** each subject gets.
:::

{{< practice >}}

Work with a partner. Compare answers when you finish each problem.

**Parts of an Experiment**

1. 60 tomato plants are randomly split into two groups of 30. One group gets a new fertilizer. The other gets only water. After 6 weeks, the weight of the tomatoes is measured.

   a. What are the subjects?

   b. What is the explanatory variable?

   c. What is the response variable?

   d. What is the control group?

   e. Why split the plants **randomly**?

2. In the headache experiment, the study is double-blind.

   a. Why should the subjects not know which pill they got?

   b. Why should the nurses who measure headache relief not know?

***

**Designing Experiments**

3. Does listening to music help students memorize a list of words? You have 50 student volunteers. Describe a completely randomized experiment. Name the treatments, how you assign them, and what you measure.

4. A company tests two hand lotions. Each of 20 volunteers puts Lotion A on one hand and Lotion B on the other. A coin flip decides which hand gets A. After a week, a doctor rates the dryness of each hand.

   a. What kind of design is this?

   b. Why flip a coin to pick the hand?

   c. Why is this design better than giving 10 people Lotion A and 10 people Lotion B?

5. A teacher tries a new reading program with her 1st-hour class and the old program with her 6th-hour class. The 1st-hour class scores higher. Can she conclude the new program works better? Explain.

6. A school tests a reading program. It splits students by grade, then randomly assigns half of each grade to the program.

   a. What kind of design is this?

   b. Why split by grade first?
